failing_part: gives an approximately valid 95% interval, because repeating the folds 10 times makes the fold differences approximately independent
narrowest_regime: None for the naive t. The 50 fold differences share overlapping training sets and each repeat re-tests the same n rows, so they are positively correlated and s2_d/(rK) badly understates the variance of the mean difference. A variance-corrected t (Nadeau-Bengio: s2_d*(1/rK + n_test/n_train)) is the usual repair.
reason: Repeating K-fold does not make the differences independent: training sets overlap by about (K-2)/(K-1) within a repeat and every repeat reuses the same data, so the effective sample is nearer the n units than 50 pairs, and the mean difference has far more variance than s2/50 implies. In a simulation with labels independent of features (true accuracy difference exactly 0 for any learners), the 10x5 naive paired t at the 5% level rejected in 49% (n=100) and 58% (n=300) of 500 datasets, while the Nadeau-Bengio corrected t rejected 1.0% and 5.4%. Dietterich (1998) and Bouckaert & Frank (2004) report this inflation; they do not support the claim.

citations.cite: Dietterich 1998, Neural Computation 10:1895-1923 (shows the resampled/repeated-CV paired t has inflated Type I error)
Bouckaert & Frank 2004, PAKDD (replicability of tests; repeated CV t-tests with independence assumed are unreliable)
Nadeau & Bengio 2003, Machine Learning 52:239-281 (corrected resampled t-test)

bite_note: A naive 49-df interval is far too narrow, so the researcher would call a model difference real about half the time when there is none; the choice of interval changes the verdict on which family is better.

failing_part: fitting once at the library's default settings with no search ... predicts at least as well as nested tuning and is better calibrated
narrowest_regime: No regime established. Defaults might tie tuning only where the tuning space has no regularizing candidates or the inner CV is unusable (very few events); the penalized-regression literature on tuning-parameter variance does not transfer to boosted-tree defaults.
reason: In simulation (logistic outcome, 10 predictors with interactions and nonlinearity, 40 replicates per cell, 20000 test rows) a nested random search of 8 candidates scored by 3-fold log loss beat the library defaults in every cell: HistGB at n=200-300 cut test log loss by 0.03-0.18 and Brier by 0.001-0.047 and raised calibration slope from about 0.16-0.57 to 0.59-0.91; XGBoost defaults (eta 0.3, depth 6) were worse still (log loss 0.93 vs 0.65 at n=200); a rare-outcome table (n=2000, about 180 events, so n_plan < 300) gave the same result. The defaults overfit badly at this size, so the selection variance the claim cites is smaller than the overfitting bias it avoids. The cited Riley/Van Calster/Martin work concerns penalized regression, not boosted trees.

citations.cite: Van Calster, van Smeden, De Cock, Steyerberg 2020, Stat Methods Med Res 29:3166-3178 (shrinkage for regression models does not guarantee improvement; about regression, not boosting)
Martin, Riley, Collins, Sperrin 2021, Stat Methods Med Res 30:2545-2561 (bootstrap variability of tuning parameters; penalized regression)
Riley et al. 2021, J Clin Epidemiol 132:88-96 (penalization unreliable when sample small; regression models)

bite_note: The app would skip the search (S=0) for every boosted-tree fit below n_plan 300 and deliver a model with a calibration slope near 0.3-0.5 and worse log loss than a tuned one; the decision changes both discrimination and calibration of the delivered model.

failing_part: a standard regression that adjusts for the confounder at every time point gives an unbiased estimate of the total effect of the exposure history, so marginal structural models are needed only to gain efficiency
narrowest_regime: Only when the confounder is not affected by prior exposure (no treatment-confounder feedback), or when the target is a controlled direct effect of a single time point holding others fixed under extra assumptions; with exposure-affected time-varying confounding conventional adjustment is biased for the total effect.
reason: When L_t is affected by earlier exposure A_{t-1}, it is both a confounder of later exposure and a mediator of the earlier exposure's effect. Adjusting for it blocks part of the effect of A_{t-1} (over-adjustment of the total effect) and, if an unmeasured cause U of L_t and the outcome exists, opens a collider path A_{t-1} -> L_t <- U -> Y; not adjusting leaves confounding. No standard outcome regression can fix both, which is why g-methods (MSM with IPW, g-formula, g-estimation) were developed for bias, not efficiency. Robins, Hernan & Brumback 2000 states exactly this and says the opposite of the claim.

citations.cite: Robins, Hernan & Brumback 2000, Epidemiology 11:550-560, Marginal structural models and causal inference in epidemiology
Hernan & Robins 2020, Causal Inference: What If, ch. 19-21 (time-varying treatments, treatment-confounder feedback)

bite_note: The app would recommend ordinary time-varying-adjusted regression instead of an MSM or g-formula; in feedback settings that returns a biased total effect, often even the wrong sign.

failing_part: losing more than 10% of the rows ... is enough to warrant a concern
narrowest_regime: As a screening trigger for a kept-vs-dropped check it is a reasonable rule of thumb (it costs the researcher one table). It is not a measure of bias: the concern depends on the missingness mechanism and whether it relates to the outcome given the model's covariates, plus on the absolute number of rows left.
reason: Complete-case bias depends on the mechanism, not the share dropped. In a simulation (n=2000, true slope 1.0) dropping 30% of rows completely at random, or 27% depending only on the predictor, left the slope unbiased (0.999-1.000), while dropping 11% depending on the outcome biased it by 11% (0.885). The 10% figure is a rule of thumb (Bennett 2001; Schafer 1999 uses 5%), not derived, and Madley-Dowd 2019 shows the missing share is a poor guide. The substantive safeguard is the kept-vs-dropped comparison the claim also includes.

citations.cite: Bennett 2001, Aust N Z J Public Health 25:464-469 (more than 10% missing is likely to bias analysis; rule of thumb)
Madley-Dowd, Hughes, Tilling, Heron 2019, J Clin Epidemiol 110:63-73 (the proportion of missing data should not be used to guide decisions)

bite_note: The warn triggers on share, so a researcher with 8% outcome-related loss sees nothing while one with 25% harmless MCAR loss sees a concern; it only changes the decision if the kept-vs-dropped comparison is read, which is the useful part.

failing_part: coding it as one indicator or as a numeric amount gives the same slope, interval and every prediction (only the intercept's reference changes)
narrowest_regime: Unpenalized (or standardized-penalty) linear/GLM fits with an intercept and tree models: predictions, fit, t and p are identical under any affine recoding. The coefficient and its interval are identical only when the two numeric values differ by exactly 1 (0/1, 1/2); in general they rescale by 1/(b-a). Penalized fits on unstandardized columns, and distance- or kernel-based learners, are not invariant.
reason: For x in {a,b}, the indicator is (x-a)/(b-a), an affine map, so predictions are unchanged in an unpenalized model with an intercept, but the slope per unit and its interval are divided by (b-a): in a check, indicator and 1/2 coding gave 1.604 (1.359, 1.850), 3/7 gave 0.401 (0.340, 0.462), -1/1 gave 0.802, with t=12.86 throughout. A ridge fit on raw columns changed predictions with the coding (row-0 prediction -0.58, -0.86, -0.89 for 0/1, 3/7, 0/100), while a standardized ridge did not. The 'combined rows: mean = share vs mode' clause is correct. The statement that both imputation models fill it as yes/no is an implementation fact I cannot check.
bite_note: Predictions and inference are unchanged for the usual unpenalized or standardized fits, so skipping the question changes nothing; it matters only if a per-unit slope is reported for non-unit spacing or an unstandardized penalized model is used.

failing_part: bounds the g-formula's Monte Carlo error from above
narrowest_regime: sd(r_i)/sqrt(n_sim) is the usual estimate of the Monte Carlo standard error of the mean when the simulated units are independent draws; it is only an upper bound (conservative) when baselines are the fixed observed cohort and r_i is a per-unit risk, because then between-baseline variation inflates sd(r_i) but is not Monte Carlo noise. It also covers one arm only and none of the model-fitting error.
reason: For iid simulated units the standard error of the mean is exactly sd/sqrt(n) (estimated), not a bound. In a simulation it matched the actual run-to-run SD (0.0192 reported vs 0.0192 actual for 0/1 events; 0.0047 vs 0.0046 for risk probabilities with resampled baselines) and fell below the actual value in 30-50% of runs. It was a genuine upper bound only for a fixed-cohort design with risk probabilities (0.0047 reported vs 0.0036 actual). Contrasts between regimens need a paired SD, not the single-arm one, and parameter uncertainty is a separate source.
bite_note: Monte Carlo error at the usual n_sim is far below sampling error, so the text's wording (estimate vs bound) does not change any decision or estimate.

failing_part: intervals that treat rows as independent would be too narrow (not universal); and the 'above 200 exposures ... refused' cap has no statistical rationale (it is a compute limit)
narrowest_regime: CR2 with Bell-McCaffrey (Satterthwaite) degrees of freedom is sound for coefficients of features that vary between units (person-level exposures), where independence-based intervals are too narrow. For a feature that varies only within units the independence-based interval is too wide, not too narrow. The 200-exposure refusal is an engineering choice, defensible only as 'do not report independence intervals', not as evidence that no valid cheaper cluster-robust interval exists.
reason: In a simulation (20 clusters of 5, ICC 0.5, true effect 0) the independence-based 95% interval for a person-level exposure covered 73.5% while CR2 + Bell-McCaffrey covered 95.6% (also 95.6% with 50 clusters), so the method choice and the 'too narrow' warning are right in that regime. For a within-cluster-only exposure the independence interval covered 99.6% (conservative) while CR2 held 95.8%. The cap of 200 is justified only by compute, and refusing leaves the researcher with nothing where CR1/CR3, wild-cluster bootstrap or CR2 on a screened subset would still be valid.

citations.cite: Bell & McCaffrey 2002, Survey Methodology 28(2):169-181 (CR2 / bias-reduced linearization and its degrees of freedom)
Pustejovsky & Tipton 2018, J Bus Econ Stat 36:672-683 (small-sample CR2 with Satterthwaite df)
Imbens & Kolesar 2016, Rev Econ Stat 98:701-712 (Bell-McCaffrey df for robust inference)

bite_note: Above 200 exposures the researcher receives no feature-wise intervals at all, whereas a cheaper cluster-robust interval would give a usable result; below 200 the CR2 choice protects coverage (73% vs 96% in the simulation).

narrowest_regime: Holds wherever within-person variance is positive (always for 24-h recalls). Caveats that do not break it: 'NCI' stands for any usual-intake measurement-error model (ISU, SPADE and MSM also qualify), and with only a handful of repeat people the adjusted distribution is unbiased on average but very noisy.
reason: Observed person means have variance sigma_b^2 + sigma_w^2/k, so any single-day or k-day-mean distribution is wider than the usual-intake distribution, which inflates both tails and the share beyond or below any cut-off. In a simulation (variance ratio 2) the single-day distribution put 28% below a cut-off whose true share is 16%, and the 2-day mean was still off (24%); a variance-component adjustment from repeat recalls was unbiased and cut the percentile error from 1.20 to 0.88 even with only 2 repeat people, 0.20 with 100. Ranking the mean-of-days view lower and showing it only beside, labeled, is a sound presentation choice.

citations.cite: Tooze et al. 2006, J Am Diet Assoc 106:1575-1587 (NCI method for episodically consumed foods)
Tooze et al. 2010, Stat Med 29:2857-2868 (NCI method for nutrients)

bite_note: Reading percentiles and the share below an EAR-type cut-off from the day-mean distribution can misstate prevalence of inadequacy several-fold (28% vs 16% in the check); the claim changes which distribution a researcher reports.

failing_part: averaging k of them cuts within-person variance k-fold
narrowest_regime: Holds exactly when the k repeats have uncorrelated errors of equal variance and every unit has k rows. With lag-1 correlation rho the variance of a k-mean is (sigma^2/k)(1 + 2*sum(1-j/k)rho^j): at rho = 0.2 and k = 4 the reduction is 1.34 times smaller than k-fold. Unequal row counts and a persistent within-person bias (day-of-week, a same-day recall) also break it.
reason: Var(mean of k) = sigma_w^2/k is the textbook result for independent replicates, so for k = 2 recalls on non-consecutive days it is nearly right; but 'repeated measurements of one quantity' covers serially correlated repeats, where the gain is smaller (e.g. 1.1x-2.0x worse than k-fold for rho 0.1-0.4), and with unequal k the average per-unit variance is sigma^2*E[1/k], not sigma^2/median(k) (0.58 vs 0.50 in an example). The between-person variance is untouched, so the mean still carries sigma_w^2/k of noise. No source is given.
bite_note: It is an explanatory coach note; for k around 2 recalls and small serial correlation the difference from an exact k-fold cut is a few percent and changes no choice.

failing_part: one input's share is said to be unstable when the reseeds' rank correlation is under 0.7
narrowest_regime: The first two clauses (SHAP/ALE describe the fitted model, not the effect of intervening; credit within a correlated group is not identified) hold in general. The 0.7 reseed rank-correlation rule is a convention with no derivation, and as a per-row rank correlation it does not detect an arbitrary split.
reason: The conceptual parts match Lundberg & Lee, Apley & Zhu and Molnar et al. (SHAP and ALE are model descriptions; correlated features share credit non-identifiably). But no reason is given for 0.7, and a reseed check is a weak detector of the arbitrariness, which comes from the data and model class rather than the seed. In a simulation with two equally causal predictors (rho 0.99; random forest and boosting, 5 seeds), the per-row Spearman correlation of x1's SHAP across seeds was 1.00 while x1's share of the pair's credit ranged 0.40-0.49 across seeds (boosting gave a seed-invariant 0.30 vs the true 0.50), so the rule would call it stable.

citations.cite: Lundberg & Lee 2017, NeurIPS (SHAP)
Apley & Zhu 2020, JRSS-B 82:1059-1086 (ALE)
Molnar et al. 2022, xxAI LNCS 13200:39-68, General pitfalls of model-agnostic interpretation methods (correlated features, causal misreading)

bite_note: The flag decides whether an input's credit is shown as stable or caveated in the 'what drives it' reading; a researcher told it is stable would read a single input's share from a correlated group as meaningful.

narrowest_regime: Holds as a conservative wording policy. 'Trials' should mean randomized assignment, and even there causal wording attaches to the assigned intervention (intention-to-treat), not to post-randomization subgroups or mediators; the claim states only a necessary condition, so this does not break it.
reason: The tiering matches standard causal-inference practice: an adjusted observational estimate is an association unless the causal contrast, identifying assumptions (exchangeability, positivity, consistency) and design are stated; an 'estimated effect, its assumptions named' middle tier is the target-trial/g-methods convention; randomized assignment is what licenses unqualified causal wording; and SHAP/ALE-type model explanations describe the fitted function, not an intervention. 'No stated assumption refuted' is a weak but not wrong gate, because untestable assumptions cannot be confirmed, only contradicted by checks. The cited basis is an internal ruling, so the support is the methods reasoning, not the citation.

citations.cite: Hernan 2018, The C-word, Am J Public Health 108:616-619 (causal intent should be stated with assumptions rather than hidden behind association language)
Hernan & Robins 2020, Causal Inference: What If (identification conditions; target trial emulation)

bite_note: It decides which sentence the Results draft offers and whether stronger user wording is flagged; an observational adjusted estimate would otherwise be written as 'X affects Y' or, in the other direction, as a bare association.

failing_part: Dietary data with total energy and at least two macronutrient totals in grams (the 0.90-1.10 band assumes the Atwater reconstruction covers protein, carbohydrate and fat)
narrowest_regime: The ratio logic is sound when protein, carbohydrate and fat are all present (kcal ratio about 1.0, kJ about 4.18, N-day mismatch about N; a 4-day kcal total at 4.00 vs kJ 4.184 is a 4.4% gap, so the 5% overlap rule is correct arithmetic, and a ratio near 1 cannot reveal the day count when energy and macros span the same days).
reason: With only two of the three energy macronutrients the reconstruction omits a large part of energy, so correct single-day kcal data do not land in 0.90-1.10: with typical US shares (protein 16%, carbohydrate 49%, fat 33%) the ratio is about 2.0 for protein+fat, 1.5 for protein+carbohydrate and 1.2 for carbohydrate+fat. The protein+fat case sits on the 'N = 2' ambiguity, so ordinary kcal data would be asked as a possible 2-day total, and none would be settled. The 0.90-1.10 band and the 5% tolerance are conventions (the band is wide for a 3-macronutrient check, the tolerance narrower than the band), but nothing in them is wrong.

citations.cite: Atwater general factors 4/4/9 kcal per g protein/carbohydrate/fat (alcohol 7 kcal/g omitted from the reconstruction)

bite_note: For tables with only two macronutrient columns the unit/day-count question is raised spuriously (or the band never settles), blocking or interrupting energy-based screens until answered; with all three macronutrients nothing changes.
